body: Sully’s on a playoff Saturday is black and gold from the green awning in. The shamrock in the window still has its one leaf out, and under it the place is packed to the walls with people who sound like Lena or like her cousins, standing three deep at the bar for a game that hasn’t started. The big screen at the back has the Superdome from the blimp. The five tube televisions up in the corners have it smaller, in five slightly different greens. Somebody has taped a fleur-de-lis cut out of a pizza box to the register.

One of the tubes, the one over the kitchen door, isn’t on the game. It’s on CNN with the sound off, because Lena asked the owner, and by now he says yes to her about everything. Port-au-Prince from a helicopter: the airport with its one runway and a gray cargo plane sitting on it, more planes up in the haze waiting their turn, pallets of water shrink-wrapped on the tarmac in the sun and going nowhere. A man on a street holds a plastic jug up to the camera, upside down, to show it’s empty. The picture goes back to the helicopter. For the rest of the afternoon it’s there at the edge of Jack’s eye, over the kitchen door, whichever way he turns.

Two tables have been pushed together end to end under the brass ship’s bell, a long table with a head and a foot. At the head, under the bell, in her Brees jersey, Lena has the rope laid across both palms with the frayed end hanging over her wrist. Julian is beside her in a gray cardigan with a borrowed Brees jersey pulled on over it, a size too big, the number hanging off him. Laney is on her other side. Down the long sides: Margot, who is here, she has told everyone, for the anthropology; Kevin, and beside Kevin a girl in a 49ers cap; Joey Abruzzo, who is nineteen tomorrow and has told everyone that too. At the end of the bar, level with the foot of the table, one stool stands empty with a folded Sully’s napkin on the seat.

Skye comes in at Jack’s side in a black sweater and a gold scarf she bought at the Rite Aid on the way — “This is as far as I go,” she told him in the car — and Theo comes in behind them in the navy blazer, straight from a pledge breakfast, with Hollis riding in his teacup. Up at the head of the table Lena sees them. She leans to Laney and says something short. Jack can’t hear it over the pregame. Laney nods.
Then Lena ties the rope off to the cleat on the post and comes down the long side of the table to meet them.
“Skye,” she says. “Welcome.”
“Lena.”

body.text: “Thank you for the thank-you,” Skye says.

body: “Y’all take the foot. It’s got the big screen straight on.” Lena pulls the corner chair out herself and sets it facing the screen, and then points at the stool by the bar. “Don’t sit in Dale’s chair. He’s had it since September.”
She says all of it at an ordinary volume, with her hand on the back of the chair, and there isn’t a thing wrong with any of it. Jack would rather she’d thrown the bell at him.
“Skye, this is Julian.”
Julian stands up to shake hands. It’s a handshake you could leave your car keys with.
“The flyers,” Skye says.
“The flyers,” Julian says, pleased.

body.text: “Thanks for coming last night, Jack,” he says.
body.else: “Missed you last night, man,” he says to Jack. “Theo said you had a movie.”

body: “Loved the one about the river, Julian,” Theo says.
“Thanks, Theo.” Julian takes it as a compliment, and on him it turns into one.
Laney hasn’t gotten up. Skye goes up the table to her anyway, with something closed in her fist, and sets it down by Laney’s root beer: two little jingle bells on a pink ribbon.
“You said with bells on.”

Laney looks at the ribbon. Then she lifts one boot onto the rung of Julian’s chair, and the bells laced through her top eyelets go. “I wore my own.” She puts the ribbon in her purse, not on the table, and snaps the purse. “Word to the wise, since you brought a present. Let him win the arguments. He likes to feel tall.”
“I’ve seen your work, Price,” Jack says.

Something at the corner of Laney’s mouth starts toward the old grin and comes back. She turns to Julian. “Sugar, scoot.” Julian scoots. “Theodore, you’re over there with your friend.” She points the root beer down the table, at the foot.
Theo goes where he’s pointed. Jack takes the end chair, Skye the corner on his left, Theo the corner on his right, across from her.

Margot lifts her glass to Skye down the length of the table — subject to author — and Skye lifts hers back. Before the kickoff Skye has asked Clare about the violin, how long and who taught her and what she plays at the 11:30, and has talked to Kevin about nothing in particular — the fries, the parking, whether San Jose counts as the Bay — easily, keeping him company, until his shoulders come down from around his ears.

On Arizona’s first play from scrimmage a Cardinals running back finds a seam on the left side and is gone, most of the length of the field with nobody near him, and Sully’s goes so quiet Jack can hear the fryer.
Skye is on her feet. “He ran so *far*!”
A hundred Louisianans turn around and look at her.
“Wrong team, kid,” says a voice at her elbow. Dale has come in at the kickoff, Barry Sanders jersey and all, and he’s standing by his stool with a root beer, and he says it gently.

By the end of the Saints’ first drive Dale and Joey are teaching her the chant, one on each side of her, Joey at full Staten Island and Dale under his breath — *Who dat* — and she gets it wrong three new ways and then right, and does it at the big screen with both fists, and the next table over turns around and does it back at her.

When the Saints punt she cheers that too, because it went so high. Dale explains punting to her, patiently, as a form of giving up. She says it’s the saddest thing in sports. Dale says she hasn’t met the Lions.

Between plays she adopts Dale. Jack watches it happen. She asks where Warren is, and Dale says Michigan, not the other one, and she asks what he did there, and he says Warren Truck, twenty-seven years on the line, Dodge Rams. Instead of saying *oh*, she asks him what the line sounds like at shift change.
Dale thinks about it. “Like church letting out,” he says. “Everybody talking at once.”
“And the first Monday after?”
Dale lifts his chin at the screen and watches the Saints line up. “Got up at a quarter to five,” he says. “Habit.” He drinks his root beer, and that’s the answer.
Jack knows that chin. He has eaten breakfast across from it.
Joey climbs onto the rung of his chair with his root beer in the air. “Tomorrow I’m nineteen,” he tells Sully’s, “and in eight years I’m a priest!”
The next table cheers. Somebody at the bar yells *Father Joey*.
“Can priests watch football?” Skye asks him.
“Father Osei says it’s the only time he prays in Twi.”

Halfway down the table Clare is explaining the nickel to Kevin. “Five defensive backs. They take a linebacker off. It’s third and long, they want speed.” She has four brothers in San Jose; she mentions them like a varsity letter. Kevin nods, and tells her about concussions — the brain moving inside the skull, the cumulative effect, a study out of Boston — through two plays and part of a third, and Clare listens to every word of it with her cap pushed back and asks him a good question at the end.

The Saints answer. Brees takes them the length of the field in a handful of plays, and they score, and at the head of the table Lena is up under the bell with the rope unhitched and in both hands, and the brass goes over and back and shouts, and the bar shouts with it. Jack watches the bell. Skye watches Lena: both hands on the rope, ringing one pull past where anybody would stop, and one more, with her eyes on the screen. Skye watches it to the last pull. Then she turns back to Dale and asks him whether Lions fans have a chant.
Late in the first quarter the Saints have the ball, third-and-four, and Arizona calls time out, and Joey crosses himself.
Skye sees it. “Wait. Is that *allowed*?”
“Is what allowed?” says Joey.
“Praying for a first down.” She turns in her chair. “Is it? You’d know. Is God allowed to care about third-and-four?”
“It’s allowed,” Jack says. “It’s just not how it works. He’s not a vending machine. You don’t put in a Hail Mary and get a first down.”

“Why not?” She points her root beer at him. “Your Chesterton. Chapter four. Grown-ups get bored, so they decide God must be bored, so they decide the sun comes up because it has to. And he says maybe it’s the other way. Maybe God’s like a little kid who says *Do it again* to the sun every morning. Maybe He makes every daisy separately and never gets tired of it.” The bottle swings to the big screen. “A God who makes every daisy separately can care about third-and-four.”
Up the table Julian laughs, surprised into it.
“Chesterton was talking about the sun,” Jack says. “Not the Cardinals.”
“You pray for parking.”
“St. Anthony’s for lost things. Parking is a lost thing.”

body.text: “Two thousand years slower, you said.” She leans in across the corner of the table. “Third down is *right now*.”
“And Wednesday you said you don’t know.” She leans in across the corner of the table. “So you don’t know about third down.”
“Ask Becca’s grandmother,” she says, and leans in across the corner of the table, delighted to be handing him his own line.
“Becca’s grandmother would pray for a field goal.”

body: “She’s *right*, Jack!” Joey tells the bar. Margot has turned her chair all the way around to face the foot of the table and is following every exchange with her head, deadpan, delighted. Kevin has gone quiet over his plate of fries.
From his stool, without taking his eyes off the screen, Dale says, “My Lions prayed. Didn’t take.”

They go at it hard and laughing, Skye up on one knee on her chair, Jack with his elbows on the table, and the timeout runs long for a truck commercial, and the table has stopped pretending to watch the truck.
At the head of the table Lena has the rope across her knees, and her hands have gone still on it. She is watching the truck commercial on the big screen as though there will be a quiz on it.

journal.title: Clare Dominguez
journal.text: Clare Dominguez. Newman sophomore. Plays violin in the Mass band. Played ‘Ashokan Farewell’ at the Haiti table and people stopped on the lawn. Kevin’s mother knows her mother. Everybody’s mother knows her mother. Four brothers, back in San Jose. Knows football better than Kevin. Wore a 49ers cap to Sully’s.

journal.title: Dale (Sully’s)
journal.text: Dale Wisniewski. A Lions fan alone at the end of Sully’s bar in a Barry Sanders jersey. Warren, Michigan — not the other one. Tips in quarters. Said the rookie’s going to be good. Lions 38, Browns 37, on the last play. He bought me a root beer: the only man in California who knows what that cost. The playoffs: Skye adopted him. She asked him about shift change at Warren Truck. Nobody ever asks him about shift change.

journal.title: Julian Park-Ellis
journal.text: Julian Park-Ellis. The guitar guy from the Lighthouse stairs. Plays Bastille Thursdays. Wrote a song called “Fresno.” Plays it once a month. All Souls: came to St. Brendan’s to write Nora Calloway’s name in the book. She was his friend. They sang together. He saw us leave in the second chorus. Something new Thursday. A handshake you’d trust with anything. Sunday he came to the nine o’clock with Lena. Didn’t receive. Had the Sanctus by ear by the end. Picked Lena up at twenty to twelve for the vampires, straight from Bastille. Friday he brought her juk in his mother’s thermos and asked her what she’d go to jail for, and listened to all of it. Drove down from Oakland for the nine o’clock; his brother Daniel’s home from the Navy. Two coffees on the wall. Asked me to stay to the end of the new one. Thursday at Bastille: it’s called ‘Magdalena.’ It’s good. The Advent party: plays piano too, by ear. Under contraband mistletoe he kissed her cheek. Kissed her goodbye at his car, for Oakland. Asked me to make sure she eats before her flight. In sixty-one pictures from Lucille’s baptism, at the Broussards’ table between Mémère and Josie. Tess’s caption calls him *le petit violon*. Flew home to Oakland on the fourth. Tuesday morning, on the feed: a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late; Lena tagged. Songs for Haiti, Friday at Bastille, every dollar to CRS. Theo asked him how many are about her. ‘One.’ Friday at Bastille, for Haiti: a new one, about New Year’s on a river. At Sully’s Lena introduced him to Skye. ‘The flyers.’

choices.text: “He doesn’t take sides in a football game. There are Catholics in Arizona.”
response: “He doesn’t take sides in a football game,” Jack says. “There are Catholics in Arizona.”
“There were Egyptians at the Red Sea,” Skye says, “and He picked a side.”

Joey whoops. She isn’t finished. She sweeps the bottle at the room — the table, the bar three deep, the hundred black-and-gold backs, the bell. “And these people. Their city went under the water. Four years of novenas and candles and a football team on its back, and you’re telling me He looks down at all of that and says, *Sorry, I don’t do sports*?”
Jack looks up the table to the head of it, to the girl under the bell.
Skye sees him do it. She looks where he looked, up the length of the table, and then back at the big screen.

The timeout ends. Brees takes the snap on third-and-four and finds a man in the end zone, and Sully’s comes up out of its chairs, and Lena is on her feet with the rope, and the bell goes over, and that’s the end of the argument.

choices.text: “If prayer moved the line, Cleveland would have a parade.”
response: “If prayer moved the line,” Jack says, “Cleveland would have a parade.”
“Detroit’d have two,” Dale says from the bar.

“Cleveland didn’t pray hard enough.” Skye turns in her chair and holds the bottle out at the room like a microphone — at the table, at the bar three deep, at the bell. “You know who did? These people. Their city was underwater. Four years of novenas and candles and a football team on its back, and He looks down at all that and goes, *Sorry, I don’t do sports*?”
Jack’s eyes go up the table to the head of it, to the girl under the bell.
Skye sees them go. She turns her head and looks where he’s looking, and then at the big screen.

On third-and-four Brees drops back and throws, and the ball comes down in the end zone in somebody’s hands, and the bar goes up all at once, and Lena is up with the rope, and the brass shouts over all of them, and nobody is arguing about anything anymore.

choices.text: “Fine. He cares about third-and-four. He just doesn’t owe us the first down.”
response: “Fine,” Jack says. “He cares about third-and-four. He just doesn’t owe us the first down.”

“Cares, doesn’t owe.” Skye points at him. “Somebody put that on a holy card.” And she’s winning, so she keeps swinging. “And if He cares about third-and-four, look where you are.” The bottle takes in the room: the table, the bar three deep, the bell. “These people’s city went under the water. Four years of novenas and candles and a football team on its back. You think He looked at all that and said, *Sorry, I don’t do sports*?”
Jack’s eyes go to the head of the table. Lena is under the bell with the rope across her knees.
Skye watches his eyes go. She follows them up the table, and then puts her own back on the game.

The Saints come out of the timeout and Brees converts it and then some — into the end zone — and the place stands up roaring, and Lena is on her feet with the rope in both hands, and the bell takes the argument away from all of them.

s09b.slug: SATURDAY · 2:12 PM · SULLY’S, THE LONG TABLE
body: The extra point is good, and the broadcast goes to commercial, and the last of the bell is still up in the rafters with the neon. Skye stands and pats her pockets. “I need reinforcements,” she says, and goes up to the bar for root beers. Julian’s phone goes in his cardigan; he looks at it and says, “Oakland,” to Lena, and takes it out the front door. Through the window Jack can see his back on the sidewalk under the awning, the phone at his ear, one hand pushed up into his hair.

Up at the taps Skye has the bartender laughing inside of a minute. A girl in a Reggie Bush jersey leans over from the next stool and asks her something, and Skye says, “Only on Thursdays,” and the girl shrieks and grabs her friend, and Skye signs a Sully’s coaster for her with the bartender’s pen and slides a dollar into the tip jar on top of it. From the foot of the table Jack watches her lean on the bar on her elbows, the gold scarf coming undone, one boot heel hooked on the brass rail, saying something to the bartender that makes him put both hands over his face. Half of him is simply glad: glad of her, of the noise she makes in a room, of the fact that she’s here, in this one, on a Saturday. Laney is watching her too, the whole way to the taps and back down the bar again, with her chin on the heel of her hand.

At the head of the table Lena has turned in her chair toward the tube over the kitchen door. The helicopter again, the runway again, a line of people along a wall with buckets. She watches it with the rope across her lap and her thumbs on the knot at the end of it.

It’s the dead minute after a score, when a bar this full goes as quiet as it ever goes: ice, the fryer, a chair. Laney doesn’t lower her voice. She has never in her life lowered her voice. She leans back and says it to Lena.
“Oh my God. He found a California you. Excuse me while I go be a bitch on your behalf.”

It reaches the foot of the table without trying. At the head of it Lena’s hand stays where it is on the bell rope, and she doesn’t look down the table, and Skye comes back from the bar with two root beers sweating in her fists.

Laney waits until she’s sitting. “Loved your picture this morning,” she says down the table, sweet as tea. “So candid. Kenzie Rourke had it on her phone before I’d had my coffee. Who does your candids?”
“My arm,” Skye says, and holds the arm up and turns it in the light, like something she won at a fair.
“And is he a series regular,” Laney says, “or more of a guest arc?”

Under the table Skye’s hand finds Jack’s knee and grips it, hard enough to hurt. He can feel each of her fingers separately, and the nails through his jeans. Above the table she is smiling with every tooth she owns, and nothing about her shoulders has moved at all.
“Series regular,” she says. “They picked up the back nine.”

Down the table the jab has landed on everybody. Joey is looking hard at his fries. Margot has her eyebrows up and her pen still. Kevin opens his mouth — “Respectfully, Laney —” — and Clare, without seeming to do anything, puts her hand on his sleeve, and he shuts it again.

Laney turns to Julian, who has come back in from the sidewalk with his phone still in his hand, and asks him how his mother is. Skye twists around on her chair to Dale at the bar behind her and asks him what a nickel is, and Dale starts to tell her. Across the corner of the table Theo leans in to Jack and says it low, for Jack and nobody else:
“She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.”

He sits back and straightens a cuff and looks at the screen. It’s short, for Theo. When Theo lies he furnishes it, down to the drapes; when he means a thing it comes out small. Jack can’t tell which way this one cuts, toward her or toward him, and Theo has already gone back to the game.

It comes up the back of Jack’s neck before he knows what it is — heat, under his collar, into his ears, the place on his knee where her fingers dug in still singing with it. He has been a lot of things with Laney Price since August. Scared of her. Bossed by her. Saved in his phone because she put herself there. Never this. Up the table the bells on her boots go when she crosses her legs, and the little sound goes straight up his spine. He looks up the table for the reason and finds Julian’s arm along the back of Lena’s chair, and Lena’s hand on the rope, and Laney asking after somebody’s mother in Oakland, and the two girls at that end cold to him all week for a reason neither of them will say. He has a sentence for Laney. He has several. Under the table his own hand has found the edge of the seat and is holding it, and he keeps every one of them behind his teeth.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’

choices.text: *To the table, not to Laney:* “She’s not a guest.”
choices.key: At Sully’s, when Laney took her shot at Skye, you told the table Skye isn’t a guest.
response: “She’s not a guest,” he says.

Not to Laney. To the table — to the ketchup and the root beers and the Superdome on the big screen — at an ordinary volume, and the table hears it. Joey says “Amen” by reflex, and then looks at his root beer as if it said it. Skye’s grip on his knee lets go. Her hand stays, and her thumb goes back and forth across the place where the nails were. At the head of the table the bell rope gives a small jerk, and settles. Theo picks up his root beer and drinks to nobody in particular.
Laney is looking at him. Not at Skye; at him. Whatever is on his face, she gets all of it, and for once she has nothing to say.

choices.text: *Put your hand over hers on your knee. Eyes on the screen.*
choices.key: At Sully’s, when Laney took her shot at Skye, you put your hand over hers under the table and said nothing.
response: He puts his hand over hers on his knee and keeps his eyes on the big screen, where a lizard with an English accent is selling car insurance. Her fingers turn over under his and lace in and grip. Above the table, with her free hand, she lifts her root beer up the table at Laney — a little toast, every tooth still showing — and drinks. He watches the commercial to the end. He watches the kickoff after it. He couldn’t say who kicked.
When he finally looks up the table, Laney is already looking at him. She has been since the commercial started. She doesn’t look away when he catches her at it.

choices.text: “Dale. Tell them what she asked you about the line.”
choices.key: At Sully’s, when Laney took her shot at Skye, you turned the table over to Dale.
response: “Dale,” he says. “Tell them what she asked you about the line.”

Dale turns around on his stool with the nickel half explained. He looks down the table at all of them. “She asked about shift change,” he says. “Twenty-seven years. Nobody in California ever asked me about shift change.” And he turns back to the bar.

The table looks at Skye a little differently after that. Margot does, anyway; she moves her chair a quarter turn toward the foot of the table and leaves it there. Skye has gone pink to the scarf. She looks at Dale’s back as if he’d pinned a corsage on her.
Laney doesn’t look at Skye at all. She’s looking at Jack, at what’s still on his face after the joke, and the joke hasn’t gotten all of it off.

choices.text: “Come on. I’ll teach you the Who Dat properly.”
choices.key: At Sully’s, when Laney took her shot at Skye, you took Skye up to the bar in the middle of the quarter.
response: “Come on,” he says, and stands, and the chair scrapes on the boards loud enough that Kevin jumps. “I’ll teach you the Who Dat properly.”

He takes her hand and her root beer and walks her up to Dale’s end of the bar in the middle of a Saints drive, down the length of the long table, in front of everybody, which nobody in this bar does in the middle of a drive. At the head of the table Lena keeps her eyes on the screen. At the bar he turns Skye around by the shoulders to face it and teaches her the chant right — where you take the breath, which word you lean on — and Dale beats time on the bar with his knuckles.
From there he can see the table. Laney isn’t watching the drive. She has her root beer halfway to her mouth, and she’s watching him over it, and she sets it down without drinking.

body: The 11 takes Mission Street at a Saturday crawl and stops at every corner whether anybody wants it to or not. The driver has the game on a transistor radio rubber-banded to the fare box, the Saints up by four touchdowns and the announcer already talking about next week. Across the aisle a woman sits with a laundry bag between her feet, reading a *TV Guide*. Jack sits with his temple near the window and says it under his breath to the glass: the Our Father, and then the Hail Marys, ten, counted off on his fingers against his knee, and each time he comes to *pray for us sinners* he puts her name in where the *us* goes. *Skye.* The woman turns a page. He says the Glory Be and starts over for himself, with his own name, and he’s on the eighth when the green awning goes by the window and he pulls the cord and finishes it on the sidewalk.

The game has been over since the third quarter. The Superdome on the big screen is a party with two minutes of football still to play in it — forty-five to fourteen — and Sully’s hasn’t sat down since the punt return. He stops in the doorway, under the shamrock, and not a soul in the place turns around.

The long table is on its feet. Joey is on his chair. The Saints kneel on it, and kneel on it again, and the clock runs, and the bar counts the last ten seconds down in one voice the way they do in Times Square, and at the gun Lena has the rope in both hands under the bell.
She turns, and holds it out down the table. To Skye.
“Our guest,” she says.

Skye looks at the rope, and takes it, and rings that bell like the building is on fire. The brass goes over and back and over, and the table comes in under it with the chant — *Who dat, who dat* — and Laney is looking at Lena, not at the bell, and Dale at the end of the bar has put his root beer down to applaud with both big hands, and Theo is standing at the foot of the table, clapping slowly, his face beautifully arranged.

Lena sees him first. Her hand is still out where the rope was, open and empty, and over Skye’s shoulder she finds him in the doorway; the hand comes down, and closes, and she reaches past Julian for her jacket on the back of the chair.
Skye sees him a heartbeat later. She holds the rope up at him over everybody’s heads like a prizefighter’s belt and rings the bell one more time, just for him, and the owner lets her.

Out on the sidewalk Mission Street is honking. A pickup goes by with a fleur-de-lis bedsheet tied across the tailgate and three boys in the back yelling the chant at the stoplights. The sun is going down behind the hills, and the sky over the wharf is still light. Skye walks backward ahead of him to tell it, the gold scarf coming loose.

“Dale bought me a root beer. With *quarters*.” She drops into Michigan, flat as a parking lot, chin up at an invisible screen: “*Kid’s a natural.*” And back. “He said that. To the bartender. Not even to me. Joey says I’m going to be a Catholic by the Super Bowl, and I said I’m a Saints fan now, isn’t that most of it, and Joey had to sit down, and Ted said Joey should be a bishop.” She stops walking backward and just walks, beside him, her arm through his. “The redhead smiled once. Ted has witnesses.”
“Once?”

“Once. In the fourth quarter. At Dale.” She tips her head onto his shoulder for half a block. “Kevin explained what a concussion is to me. Twice. Clare held my hand under the table for the second one. Joey wrote the chant on a coaster in case I forget it overnight.” She pulls the coaster out of her back pocket to prove it: WHO DAT, in ballpoint capitals, and under it a phone number with a 718 area code. “That’s his mom’s. In case of emergency. And then at the end they gave me the bell.”
She stops on the sidewalk outside a dry cleaner’s and turns him around by the arm to face her, and she’s lit up from the inside like a jukebox.
“Jack. That’s the best thing anybody’s ever handed me in a bar.”

A car honks at them, for the Saints, and she kisses him on Mission Street anyway, and somebody leaning out the passenger window yells *who dat*, and she yells it back without quite taking her mouth off his.

They eat burgers on the hood of the Saab in the lot behind the wharf while the flags go by out on Mission, and then she drives the coast road north with the windows down and nowhere to be until the last light is off the water. By the time she turns onto Del Playa it’s nearly ten, and down at the Las Olas end of Seacliff Lupe’s white truck is just pulling in to put its lights up.
